source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: Benchmark of LLM agents on four fault-management tasks: detect, localize, root-cause, mitigate. Agents beat classic non-LLM AIOps tools on detection and localization. Root cause and mitigation are hardest.
numbers: Overall accuracy: GPT-4 w/ shell 49.15%, GPT-3.5 w/ shell 15.25%, ReAct 55.93%, FLASH 59.32% (step limit 20). Detection: ReAct 76.92%, GPT-4 69.23%, GPT-3.5 23.07%. RCA: ReAct 45.45%, GPT-4 40.90%, GPT-3.5 9.09%. Mitigation (row order read from garbled table): ReAct 54.55%, FLASH 36.36%, GPT-4 27.27%, GPT-3.5 0%.
limits: Small problem set: the percentages imply about 13 detection, 13 localization, 22 RCA, 11 mitigation items. Simulated microservice apps, not real plants. Table columns were garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Fault management is the same loop as Woods's anomaly response (notice, localize, explain, act). Later stages fail most, so an impasse detector should weight them.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: Accuracy rises with step budget for ReAct and FLASH but plateaus fast for GPT-3.5. Extra steps only burn tokens. Authors say self-repair from environment feedback saturates in ops tasks, unlike coding where tests keep giving signal.
numbers: FLASH reaches 59.32% at step limit 20. GPT-3.5: no gain beyond 5 steps.
limits: Only 4 agents; step limit varied 3 to 20.
agent_relevance: Budget alone does not fix stuck behaviour (Woods 'decompensation': effort without change). Count progress, not steps.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: Observed agent failure behaviours: repeating the same API call, inventing non-existent APIs, repeating the same malformed call, flooding context with raw telemetry, and false positives on detection.
numbers: GPT-3.5 repeated the same malformed call up to 14 times inside one 20-step case, often replying 'I apologize for the error. Here is the API call again'. In multi-agent chat, one agent spoke ten times in a step with no communication.
limits: Qualitative, from logs of the authors' own agents.
agent_relevance: Direct machine analogue of Woods 'stuck in outdated behaviour': same action, same error. Detector rule: identical action plus identical error N times.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: The 'is anything wrong?' step is not trivial for models. Per the text, only FLASH answered all detection problems correctly, and false-positive detection was a flagged issue.
numbers: Detection accuracy: FLASH 100% (per text); ReAct 76.92%; GPT-4 69.23%; GPT-3.5 23.07%.
limits: Table row labels garbled; FLASH 100% rests on the paper's text statement.
agent_relevance: Anomaly detection needs a baseline of normal. Our agent should be able to say 'no anomaly' without being forced to fix something.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Grounded-theory failure taxonomy from 150 traces, then 1642 annotated traces over 7 multi-agent frameworks. 14 failure modes in 3 groups: system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification.
numbers: 1642 traces, 7 frameworks, failure rates 41% to 86.7% across frameworks. Human agreement kappa=0.88 (3 annotators, 15 traces). LLM judge (o1) vs humans kappa=0.77, accuracy 94%; unseen systems kappa=0.79. Group shares 41.8% design, 36.9% misalignment, 21.3% verification.
limits: Authors say the taxonomy is not exhaustive. Annotation at scale is by an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Gives machine counterparts to Woods patterns: Step Repetition (FM-1.3) is stuck in outdated behaviour; Reasoning-Action Mismatch (FM-2.6); No or Incorrect Verification (FM-3.2/3.3); Unaware of stopping conditions (FM-1.5).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Rates of modes relevant to impasse detection: step repetition, unaware of stopping, reasoning-action mismatch, premature termination, missing or wrong verification.
numbers: Per text: step repetition 15.7%, unaware of stopping conditions 12.4%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, premature termination 6.20%, no or incomplete verification 8.20%, incorrect verification 9.10%, fail to ask clarification 6.80%, task derailment 7.40%.
limits: Shares of annotated failures; modes co-occur. Figure and text numbers for FM-1.3 to 1.5 were scrambled in extraction, so mapping follows the text order.
agent_relevance: Step repetition is common and code-detectable (hash of last actions). Verification gaps are a large group, matching G2 and G3.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Two small interventions on ChatDev show design fixes help but do not solve the problem.
numbers: Clearer role specification: +9.4% task success (GPT-4o). Adding a high-level task-objective verification step on ProgramDev: +15.6%.
limits: One framework, one benchmark; authors say isolated fixes are not enough.
agent_relevance: Cheap structural checks beat more prompting. A verification step tied to the task objective is a scaffold element, not a persona.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM Agents Fail and How They Can Learn from Failures (AgentDebug)
finding: Modular error taxonomy (memory, reflection, planning, action, system) and a benchmark of annotated failure trajectories from ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop. A debugger that finds the root-cause step and gives targeted feedback lets agents recover.
numbers: AgentErrorBench: AgentDebug all-correct 24.3% vs 0.3% for direct prompting; step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0%. GAIA step accuracy 58.0% vs 30.0%. Re-running with its feedback: up to 26% relative gain in task success.
limits: Annotations and feedback are LLM generated; gains larger for smaller models.
agent_relevance: Cascading errors map to Woods 'cross purposes' and garden-path failures. Locate the first wrong step with code help, then feed back only real failing output (G2).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When)
finding: Automated failure attribution in multi-agent LLM logs is hard. Models are poor at pointing to the decisive error step.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems. Best method: 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level. Some methods below random. Even o1 and R1 not practical. All-at-once best for agent-level, step-by-step best for step-level; accuracy falls as context grows.
limits: Human-annotated dataset; 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis of 'where did it go wrong' is the weak skill, as with human operators who misattribute. Do not trust a model to locate its own error without a check.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and fix its answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it helps a lot, so the gain comes from knowing when the answer is wrong.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic, GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after 2 rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 84.3/89.7/29.0; GPT-4 97.5/85.5/59.0.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Reasoning tasks without tools; earlier models; table layout garbled, mapping inferred from column order.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: revise only after a real failure signal. A detector that fires on a check, not on a schedule, is the machine version of 'something is off'.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey finds no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM, except in tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Qualitative survey; three headline conclusions.
limits: Covers work to 2024; later reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: Detect with code or tools; correct with the model. Same split as our schema (program decides, model fills a slot).

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based Agents for Root Cause Analysis
finding: ReAct agent (GPT-4) with retrieval tools on Microsoft cloud incidents is competitive with retrieval-only and chain-of-thought baselines and hallucinates far less, but gives up more often.
numbers: Manual labels of 97 cases: correct 39% (retrieval k=10 and CoT) vs 35% ReAct. Hallucination: 40% retrieval, 12% CoT, 4% ReAct. Of incorrect predictions, 66% of ReAct say insufficient information vs 32% CoT and 18% retrieval. 28 of 97 solved by all three.
limits: One company's internal incidents; manual coding on about 100 predictions per model; zero-shot ReAct; lexical metrics near flat.
agent_relevance: ReAct style gives fewer confident wrong stories (less garden path). The cost is more give-ups, so an impasse handler is needed.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based Agents for Root Cause Analysis
finding: Adding discussion comments from past incidents did not significantly help. A case study with an Azure team found the agent needs a planning tool, a human-interaction tool, and visible tool errors.
numbers: Agent struggled when key info (such as a cluster address) was missing from the troubleshooting guide; a planning tool made it plan before acting; tool error messages had to be shown to the agent.
limits: Case study, small, qualitative, single team.
agent_relevance: Asking a human for missing information is the designed exit from an impasse. Matches Woods's joint cognitive system view.

source: Wang et al. (2024) RCAgent: Cloud Root Cause Analysis by Autonomous Agents
finding: Industrial RCA agent with trajectory-level self-consistency, JSON regeneration, observation snapshots and expert sub-agents. Stability gains were large versus plain ReAct.
numbers: Pass rate within 15 steps: RCAgent 99.38% vs ReAct 86.33%; invalid-action rate 7.93% vs 22.82%. Nucleus sampling for the controller: pass 70.19%, invalid 44.80%. SQL tools instead of simple tools: pass 65.84%, invalid 70.94%. Self-consistency gains plateau near 20 samples; LLM aggregation beat embedding voting.
limits: Internal model and data; text-similarity metrics plus checks; not an open benchmark.
agent_relevance: Cut invalid actions with structure and simple tools before adding reflection. Voting should stay in code, and samples from one model are correlated (G4).

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI Agents across Diverse Real-World IT Automation Tasks
finding: Real-incident-based benchmark. Best agents solve few site-reliability scenarios.
numbers: 94 scenarios (SRE 42, CISO 50, FinOps 2). Resolved: SRE 13.8%, CISO 25.2%, FinOps 0%. GPT-4o SRE diagnosis pass@1 13.81% (+/-1.67), mitigation 11.43%; llama-3.3-70B 3.10%; granite-3.1-8B 3.57%; llama-3.1-8B 0.99%.
limits: 10 runs per scenario for SRE; agents are the authors' baselines; models are 2024 era.
agent_relevance: Real fault diagnosis is far below simple benchmarks, so an impasse detector should expect low base success.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI Agents across Diverse Real-World IT Automation Tasks
finding: Less observability and higher scenario complexity both cut success.
numbers: GPT-4o SRE diagnosis fell from 13.81% with traces to 9.52% without; mitigation fell to 2.86%. Success declines from Easy to Hard scenarios. FinOps cost-alert diagnosis for GPT-4o: 33%.
limits: Trace ablation on 42 scenarios (21 with, 21 without).
agent_relevance: Humans cope with partial data by gathering more. Our agent needs an 'I need data X' move (epistemic action) rather than a guess.

source: Liu et al. (2024) AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
finding: Main failure cause across interactive tasks is Task Limit Exceeded: models loop or repeat earlier content until the turn budget ends.
numbers: Table 4 (portion of outcomes, columns read as OS, DB, KG, DCG, LTP): Task Limit Exceeded 23.9, 8.0, 67.9, 0.0, 82.5 percent. Invalid Format up to 53.3% on DB. Invalid Action 10.2% on one task.
limits: Table scrambled in extraction, so column-to-task mapping is inferred; values are averages over many models including weak open ones.
agent_relevance: Running out of budget through repetition is the commonest agent failure. A repetition detector turns that into an early impasse signal.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: An existing agent loop already has an impasse trigger: if the agent repeats the same action and gets the same response more than 3 cycles, or takes more than 30 actions, it reflects and restarts with a written lesson.
numbers: AlfWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks over 12 trials. ReAct-only plateaued between trials 6 and 7 with a hallucination rate of about 22% and no recovery. Memory keeps last 3 reflections.
limits: Clean binary success signal in AlfWorld; earlier models; gains are weaker where the signal is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Closest existing LLM-agent use of Woods-style detection: a code rule (repeat count or step cap) fires a revision. Matches G1.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: A named failure mode is repeated edits to the same snippet after an errant edit. A linting guardrail that blocks bad edits raises success. Failure runs are long, success runs are short.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 18.0% with linting vs 15.0% (+/-3.0) without. 51.7% of 2,294 trajectories had at least one failed edit; eventual edit success 90.5% overall but 57.2% after one failed edit. Full test set 12.47% (286/2294).
limits: Ablation on a 300-task subset with wide error bars.
agent_relevance: Recovery gets worse the longer errors persist, as with cascading faults in Woods. Interface guardrails are cheap error containment.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When information arrives step by step, models guess early, commit to an early answer, and then rely on it. They do not recover. This is a machine form of fixation on an outdated explanation.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations; average drop 39% across six tasks vs single-turn; aptitude down about 15% but unreliability up about 112%. Recap or snowball repetition recovers only 15 to 20% of the loss.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in multi-turn conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users; sharded instructions are an artificial way to stage information; 2024-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for 'stuck in outdated behaviour' in LLMs: the first answer becomes an anchor. Rebuild from the whole evidence set instead of appending turns.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems sharply cuts accuracy. Self-consistency and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information help partly.
numbers: GSM-IC: fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently across variants (macro accuracy); the correct answer appears in 99.7% of 20-sample sets in one analysis, so the signal is present but not selected.
limits: Arithmetic only; text-davinci-003 and similar; mitigations partial.
agent_relevance: Operators face alarm floods and irrelevant data; so do LLMs. Filter telemetry in code before the model sees it (AIOpsLab shows the same flood problem).

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Models use information at the start or end of long context best and lose what sits in the middle. This hurts long diagnostic logs.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA can drop by more than 20% when the answer sits mid-context; with 20 or 30 documents it falls below the closed-book 56.1%. Longer-context version did not fix it (56.0%).
limits: QA setup, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Put the live anomaly summary at the end and keep logs short. Rebuild the alarm summary rather than appending to it.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Dataset of 13,465 prompts tests human-like biases (anchoring, status quo, primacy and others) in LLMs, with mitigation by prompt rewriting and self-help.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; commercial and open models; mitigations: zero-shot, few-shot, self-help, contrastive.
limits: Admissions-decision framing, not fault management; only abstract and setup read, effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on a first hypothesis is measurable in models. Supports asking for a rival explanation only when the detector fires, not as a ritual.

source: Woods (1994) Cognitive demands and activities in dynamic fault management: abductive reasoning and disturbance management
finding: Founding description of the human task. Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
numbers: not verified
limits: Web search quota was out, so the chapter was not reached. Citation from memory.
agent_relevance: Source of the three failure patterns and the disturbance-management loop. Needs the human-angle agent.

source: Roth, Woods and Pople (1992) Cognitive simulation as a tool for cognitive task analysis (Ergonomics 35)
finding: Older AI system built on this subfield: a cognitive simulation of operators diagnosing nuclear plant faults. Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
numbers: not verified
limits: Citation from memory only. A lead, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Lineage for a software second reader that predicts where garden-path failures arise. Worth a follow-up read.
